articles.title: Being an Entrepreneur Linked to Longer Lifespan
articles.intro: This lesson explores research linking entrepreneurship to a longer lifespan, mental health benefits, and differences among types of entrepreneurs.

sentences.text: Running your own business often means long hours, financial uncertainty and plenty of stress.
But perhaps surprisingly, it may also be linked to a longer life.
A new study of more than 27,000 older Americans found that people with entrepreneurial experience had about a 10% lower risk of death than those who worked for someone else.
The study, published in the _Journal of Business Venturing_, used data from the US Health and Retirement Study, which followed adults aged 50 and over between 1998 and 2020.
Even after things like age, earnings and past health problems were considered, the link between entrepreneurship and lower risk of death remained.
So what might be behind it?
One possible explanation is the greater control that comes with running your own business.
"Most people think of entrepreneurship as extremely stressful, and it certainly can be," said study author Cristiano Bellavitis.
"But entrepreneurship also gives people a high degree of autonomy and the opportunity to pursue something they genuinely love or care about.
Our findings suggest those benefits may have lasting effects."
The study also found that entrepreneurs had better mental health, including lower levels of depression and loneliness.
But not all entrepreneurs benefited equally.
The positive link with lifespan was concentrated among so-called "opportunity-driven" entrepreneurs — people who wanted to leave their regular job and go into self-employment.
Those who entered self-employment after losing a job did not show the same advantage.
Also, the longer people were involved in entrepreneurship, the stronger the link with longer lifespan was.
Still, that doesn't mean everyone should quit their job and start a company, Bellavitis said.
Traditional workplaces could offer some of the same benefits by giving employees more control and ownership over their work — while still offering the security of regular employment.

articles.title: More than Half of People in Japan Use AI
articles.intro: Explore how generative AI use has grown across different age groups in Japan, popular AI tools, and common uses based on recent survey data.

sentences.text: From answering questions to writing emails and helping with everyday tasks, generative AI is becoming part of day-to-day life for more people in Japan.
A new survey by the Nippon Research Center found that 56% of people aged 20 to 69 had used generative AI as of June 2026.
And for the first time, just over half of those who were surveyed said they were currently using the technology.
And it's not just young people who are using AI more.
People in their 20s were still the most likely to have tried it, at 68%, followed by those in their 30s at 61% and those in their 40s at 58%.
But older generations are catching up.
Among people in their 50s, 55% had used generative AI, while 45% of those in their 60s had tried it.
In March 2025, both groups were still at around 20%.
So which AI tools are people in Japan using?
ChatGPT was the most popular, with 30% of people saying they currently use it.
Google's Gemini was close behind at 29%, followed by Microsoft's Copilot at 15%.
The survey also looked at what people were using these tools for.
Finding information and doing research was the most common reason, mentioned by around 60% of current AI users.
Another 30% used AI to come up with ideas, while about a quarter used it to write or check emails and documents.
Interestingly, the share of people using AI for research has been growing, while the share using it to generate ideas has fallen.

articles.title: New Tour Takes Visitors Inside Japan's Northern Alps
articles.intro: Discover Japan's new Kurobe-Unazuki Canyon Route, a tour through hidden tunnels, trains, and power plants inside the dramatic Northern Alps.

sentences.text: Pack your camera — and get ready to put on a hard hat.
A new sightseeing route in Japan takes visitors deep inside the Northern Alps, where trains, tunnels and a power plant are hidden beneath the mountains.
The Kurobe-Unazuki Canyon Route opened on October 2 in Toyama prefecture.
Stretching 18 kilometers, it connects Keyakidaira Station on the Kurobe Gorge Railway with Kurobe Dam on the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route.
Visitors travel through tunnels built to carry workers and equipment for power plant construction, switching between five types of transport.
From Keyakidaira, a small train takes visitors into the mountain.
Then comes an elevator ride: 200 meters straight up through the rock.
Next, visitors board a battery-powered train — and things soon heat up!
The train passes through the "high-temperature tunnel," where temperatures reach around 40 degrees Celsius.
During construction in the 1930s, workers encountered rock as hot as 160 degrees!
At the end of the railway is the Kurobe River No. 4 Power Plant, which uses water from Kurobe Dam to generate electricity.
Completed in 1963, it was built underground to protect the landscape above.
A cable car then climbs a steep underground track, taking passengers about 450 meters higher.

From there, a 40-minute bus journey takes them toward the dam — with a chance to get the camera out as the bus stops to let visitors walk through a side tunnel to a mountain viewpoint overlooking the surrounding peaks.
Tour guide Masami Amano told _Kyodo News_ this view is her favorite part of the trip.
"It's an opportunity to view scenery that most people never will. Even experienced hikers have difficulty reaching these locations," she said.
Because the route remains a working industrial site, visitors must travel with a guide.
Packages sold through Japanese travel companies include a night's stay in Toyama City, Unazuki Onsen in Toyama prefecture, or Omachi Onsen Village in Nagano.
This year's tours run until November 30.

articles.title: _Kimjang:_ A Korean Winter Tradition
articles.intro: Explore the Korean tradition of kimjang, where families and communities prepare and share kimchi to get ready for the winter season.

sentences.text: When the weather gets colder in South Korea, some kitchens start filling up with cabbage — lots and lots of cabbage!
That's because the end of fall is the time for _kimjang_, a tradition where families and communities make and share kimchi together to prepare for winter.
The tradition is believed to have begun during Korea's Joseon Dynasty, which started in 1392 and ended in 1910.
It was difficult to grow food during winter, and people didn't have refrigerators to keep food fresh.
So, making kimchi was one way to keep vegetables for the cold months.
Over time, _kimjang_ became a community tradition, and people in villages made kimchi together.
Making kimchi takes a lot of work.
For traditional cabbage kimchi, people first put salt on the cabbage to remove some of its water.
Later, they rinse the cabbage and add a mixture that can include garlic, ginger, Korean chili powder and fish sauce.
The kimchi is then put into pots and left to ferment.
However, not everyone makes kimchi in the same way.
Different areas use different ingredients — those close to the ocean may add seafood, for example.
Families may also add their own ingredients, or have their own special ways to make kimchi.
In the past, people also had different ways to keep their kimchi cool.
Pots of kimchi could be kept underground or even hung in wells.
These days, of course, refrigerators make storing it much easier!
After a long day of making kimchi, there's traditionally something tasty waiting — boiled pork, or _suyuk_.
This is eaten while drinking {{prn:_makgeolli_ ("MAK-gol-li")|_makgeolli_}}, a Korean rice wine.
And of course, after making enough kimchi for winter, it's also time to enjoy some kimchi with this meal!

articles.title: Robert Pattinson Named as Next James Bond
articles.intro: Explore the announcement of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond and the future of the iconic film franchise.

sentences.text: Pattinson.
Robert Pattinson.
After years of speculation about who would replace Daniel Craig as the iconic secret agent, British actor Robert Pattinson has been named the next James Bond.
Amazon MGM Studios announced the decision on November 16, making Pattinson the seventh actor to play {{prn:007|double-oh seven}} in the series' 64-year history.
"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with {{prn:007|double-oh seven}} is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement.
Pattinson, 40, will star in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve.
Filming is expected to begin in 2027, although no official start date has been announced.
Villeneuve said it was a tough choice, but the right one.
"He has the timeless soul of {{prn:007|double-oh seven}} and brings a spirit that is completely new," the director said of Pattinson.

Pattinson first became internationally famous through the _Twilight_ films and has since built a varied career, appearing in major franchises such as _The Batman_, _Harry Potter_ and _Dune_, as well as smaller independent films including _The Lighthouse_ and _Mickey 17_.
He is also currently filming _The Batman Part II_.
Pattinson takes over from Daniel Craig, who played Bond in five films between 2006 and 2021.
Craig's final appearance was in _No Time to Die_, which ended with the character's death.
The film also comes at a pivotal moment for the franchise.
In 2022, Amazon bought Bond's longtime studio MGM for {{prn:$8.5 billion|eight point five billion dollars}}.
Three years later, Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson gave up creative control of the franchise.
The next installment will be the first Bond film made under Amazon's leadership.

The James Bond films, based on novels by British author Ian Fleming, have grossed more than {{prn:$7 billion|seven billion dollars}} worldwide in ticket sales, making the film series one of Hollywood's most lucrative.

articles.title: 43% of Workers Would Take a Pay Cut to Go Freelance
articles.intro: Explore why many full-time workers consider freelancing, its pros and cons, and the trend toward flexible work and self-employment.

sentences.text: Which do you prefer?
The stability and regular pay of a nine-to-five job, or the freedom and opportunity of freelance work?
If you're a full-time worker thinking about going freelance, you're far from alone.
Sharon Steiner from Fiverr, a platform for freelance workers, recently said the company's data had found that 77% of full-time workers are interested in moving to freelance work.
In fact, 67% even say they think they'll make freelancing their main job in the next three years.
Fiverr also commissioned Talker Research to survey almost 5,800 full-time workers and freelancers in the US, the UK, Canada, Germany and Australia.
The survey found that not only are many full-time workers interested in freelancing, but 43% would take a pay cut if it meant they could be their own boss.
Many full-time workers say they're actually already working a little like freelancers.
And it's not just having more flexible hours and doing more meetings over video — some full-time workers are even being paid per project instead of getting a regular salary.

It also looks like workers in general are less interested in nine-to-five jobs, with 51% of all workers saying a perfect workday actually starts before 9 a.m. — and 42% saying it should end before 5 p.m.
So it sounds like, for many, freelancing may be the answer.
But is the picture really so rosy?
Well, the Talker Research survey found that, on an average day, freelancers do have fewer meetings than full-time workers.
However, they also work two hours longer each week.
And freelancers have problems getting respect, with 29% saying they wish freelancing was seen as a real job, not just "side work."
So it's not all upsides.
The choice really depends on what's most important for you.

articles.title: Singapore Airlines Plans 'Largest Double Bed in the Sky'
articles.intro: Learn about Singapore Airlines' investment in luxury cabins, including the largest double bed in the sky and upgrades across all seating classes.

sentences.text: For most of us, getting a good night's sleep on a plane can be difficult.
But Singapore Airlines is hoping to change that — at least for passengers who can pay for a little luxury.
The airline plans to spend more than $1.5 billion on new cabins for its long-distance flights.
And the biggest attraction is what it calls "the largest double bed in the sky."
In first class, two seats next to each other will turn into a bed that's 203 centimeters long and 152 centimeters wide — the same size as a standard US queen bed.
When passengers aren't sleeping, the seats can become a sofa for two.
Each first-class cabin will also have sliding doors and 32-inch entertainment screens.
Business-class passengers will also get sliding doors and seats that turn into flat beds.
Some neighboring seats will let couples sleep side by side, too.
And people flying in economy won't be forgotten.
They'll get more legroom, better headrests and extra space for their bags.
The airline said it would also offer better in-flight entertainment, more meal options and high-speed internet.
The changes will be made to 72 planes over time, beginning in the second half of 2027.
The expensive makeover comes as airlines try to win over travelers who are happy to pay more for a better flying experience.
Air France, British Airways and other companies are also spending billions on luxury cabins.
With fuel costs going up, some travelers are choosing to stay home rather than pay higher ticket prices.
But demand for more expensive seats has stayed strong, giving airlines another reason to focus on wealthier travelers.
And if you're flying economy, here's hoping the new headrests do the trick!

articles.title: S. Koreans in Their 60s and 70s Don't Feel Old — Survey
articles.intro: A survey finds most South Koreans in their 60s and 70s don’t feel old, exploring changing views on aging, health, and staying active.

sentences.text: People often say: "You're only as old as you feel!"
And a new survey in South Korea has found that many people who are retired or almost retired don't feel old at all!
More than 500 people took part in the survey.
They were all between 60 and 74 years old.
Almost 76% of survey participants said they don't think of themselves as old.
And that went above 80% for people in their 60s.
The participants were also asked questions about what it means to be old.
Many said that if you can do everyday activities, you're not old.
Others also said that having good health means you're not old.
Sometimes, we may think of older people as needing help.
But the survey found that many older people in South Korea still want to help others.
And about two-thirds said that older people should have more chances to help others by sharing what they know.
Fifty-two percent also said they would like to learn something new.
A different survey found that one in five people in South Korea are now 65 or older.
By 2036, 30% of people in the country could be 65 or older — and that could go up to 40% by 2050.
So, with more people getting older, maybe it's time to think differently about what it means to be old!

articles.title: Japan's Household Spending Fell 6.8% in September
articles.intro: Learn about Japan's 6.8% drop in household spending, causes like weather, rising wages, inflation, and the impact of higher interest rates.

sentences.text: Household spending in Japan fell by 6.8% in September compared to one year earlier, according to government data.
It was the 10th month in a row that household spending declined.
The size of the drop surprised experts, who had predicted a 3% fall.
The decline in spending was the biggest since 2020, when spending fell because of the coronavirus pandemic.
However, real wages — the value of people's salaries adjusted for inflation — went up by {{prn:2.2%|two point two percent}} in September compared to one year earlier.
"Since wages are rising, it's hard to explain why consumer spending isn't picking up," Takeshi Minami of the Norinchukin Research Institute told _Bloomberg_.
The government blamed bad weather, such as heavy rains and typhoons, for the fall in spending, because the weather stopped people from going out.
In Tokyo, it rained every single day during the month of September — the first time this has ever happened.
Spending on dining out actually increased by 2.3%, possibly because there was a five-day holiday in September.
But spending on food and drink fell by 2.5% as the cost of a 5-kilogram bag of rice fell below 3,000 yen — about $19 — for the first time since 2024.
The Bank of Japan will have to consider this fall in spending carefully as it decides whether or not to continue raising interest rates.
Higher interest rates should help lower inflation and bring prices down, but they also make borrowing more expensive, which can impact households taking out mortgages and loans.
They also encourage people to save money rather than spend it.
The Bank of Japan has been slowly raising its interest rate to fight inflation since 2024.
In September, it rose to 1.25%, the highest rate since 1995, and it's expected to rise again in the middle of December.

articles.title: SpaceX Catches Starship Returning from Orbit for First Time
articles.intro: Explore SpaceX’s first successful catch of a returning Starship, its significance for reusable rockets, and future plans for lunar and Mars missions.

sentences.text: After circling Earth 14 times, SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned to Texas on November 14, where giant mechanical arms caught it in midair.
It was the first capture of a Starship returning from space, bringing the company closer to its goal of a fully reusable rocket system.
"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted as the spacecraft hung above the ground.
"Look at her!
Baby, she's back!"
The mission began around 22 hours earlier, when the world's largest and most powerful rocket lifted off from SpaceX's launch site near the US-Mexican border.
The rocket consists of two stages: a booster called Super Heavy that provides the initial thrust, and the Starship spacecraft mounted above it.
After separating from its booster, the spacecraft entered orbit and deployed 26 Starlink satellites.
However, SpaceX's ambition to recover both stages on the same mission ended in disappointment.
According to the company, the booster's engines stopped firing too early during its return.
Its guidance system detected that it was out of position and automatically diverted it away from the launch site.
The booster then self-destructed over the Gulf of Mexico.
Engineers are investigating the cause.
SpaceX had previously caught three boosters, but recovering both stages in a single mission remains a challenge.
Meanwhile, the company reported that the spacecraft's systems, including its protective heat shield, appeared to have performed well.
Recovering and reusing both stages could reduce costs and allow more frequent launches.
That capability would support NASA's plans for lunar exploration.
The agency is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to develop a version of Starship that can land astronauts on the moon and help establish a permanent lunar base.
In 2027, NASA's Artemis III mission is scheduled to test docking with Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon in Earth orbit.
The agency is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which would mark the first crewed moon landing since the Apollo era.
SpaceX founder Elon Musk has ambitions beyond the moon: he wants a fleet of Starships to help build a city on Mars.

articles.title: Tokyo's Akihabara Gets Solar-Powered Trash Cans
articles.intro: This lesson explores how Tokyo's Akihabara is using solar-powered, smart trash cans to address street waste with innovative technology.

sentences.text: Tourists love visiting Japan for its history, food and more.
But there's one thing many tourists don't love: there aren't many trash cans!
This isn't just a problem for tourists.
In the last few years, popular neighborhoods in Tokyo and other cities have seen an increase in trash on the streets.
However, it's not as easy as just putting a few trash cans on the corner.
Local governments have found that these trash cans quickly overflow as they're used by both people on the street and people in nearby homes, and it can be expensive to keep emptying them.
One solution is to make trash cans that don't fill up so quickly.
And one neighborhood in Tokyo is trying a high-tech solution.
Akihabara, known as one of the best places in Tokyo for technology, has put 22 solar-powered SmaGo trash cans in 10 places around the area.
These trash cans can hold much more trash than normal ones, because they can compact the trash to a fifth of its size.
They also have an online system that lets workers check how full each can is, so they know when it needs to be emptied.
The trash cans come from a Tokyo tech company called Forcetec.
Akihabara isn't the first place to get SmaGo trash cans.
They're already found in other parts of Tokyo, as well as neighborhoods in Osaka, Kyoto and other prefectures.
But it's the first time a local government in Japan has put so many of these trash cans in one place.
And Akihabara hopes they'll help keep the neighborhood clean!

articles.title: Survey Finds How Holiday Hosting Causes Stress
articles.intro: Explore how holiday hosting can cause stress, its main challenges, and tips for making gatherings more enjoyable and less overwhelming.

sentences.text: With Christmas, New Year's and many other winter holidays coming up, a lot of people have plans to host friends and family for festive fun.
However, according to a survey by Talker Research of 2,000 people living in the US, 35% find hosting people during the holidays stressful.
Chores were a major source of stress, with almost half of survey participants saying they spend more time cleaning than actually enjoying their guests' company!
Hosts were found to spend an average of 10 hours cleaning before welcoming people into their homes — and another 10 hours cleaning after they left!
This adds up to around two-and-a-half normal workdays just spent cleaning during the holidays.
And hosting comes with many more trade-offs.

Fifty-six percent of survey participants said that trying to keep their homes tidy when they had guests made them feel like they were losing quality time with their loved ones, while 36% said they had to sacrifice being able to relax.
The same percentage said cleaning meant they couldn't talk with their guests or enjoy a meal — and none of this is helped by half saying they do all the cleaning themselves.
Getting food ready can also cause a lot of stress, as 41% said they have found themselves still cooking just as guests arrive.
There are ways to lower holiday hosting stress, though.
First, you can make and follow a simple plan that gives you lots of time to do everything.
Also, try to get help — rope in others to help with cooking and cleaning, or ask everyone to bring some food and make it a potluck.
Finally, remember that holiday gatherings are about enjoying time together — and you don't need to worry about everything being perfect!

articles.title: Pink Noise Brings Better Brain-Protecting Sleep
articles.intro: Explore how pink noise during sleep may help the brain clear waste, protect against dementia, and improve deep, restorative sleep.

sentences.text: When you sleep, your brain clears out waste products such as old proteins that build up during the day.
This happens because those waste products are washed away by waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) — a clear liquid that also cushions the brain and spinal cord.
This helps keep the brain healthy and protects it against dementia.
CSF waves are at their strongest during deep sleep.
They are closely linked to a type of brain activity called slow waves, which are also strongest during this phase of sleep.
Now a new study published in _Science Translational Medicine_ has found that pink noise may strengthen those CSF waves, leading to more restorative sleep.
Pink noise is sometimes called ambient noise, and it can be used to filter out other distractions.
It uses a consistent frequency to create a flat, even sound that can be very relaxing, and often sounds a bit like steady rain or a distant waterfall.
The study monitored the brains of 14 people while they slept.
When the participants reached deep sleep, the researchers played short, 50-millisecond bursts of pink noise.
This was played quietly enough that, even though the brain registered the sound, the pink noise didn't wake anyone up.
The researchers found that pink noise seemed to increase both the strength of the brain-cleaning CSF waves during deep sleep and the associated slow wave brain activity.
The brain scans also showed how slow waves stimulated blood vessels in the brain, causing them to constrict and dilate and act like a pump driving CSF out of the brain along with waste.
The researchers now want to find out if improving CSF flow like this could help people get more restorative sleep outside of a lab setting.
This could be especially helpful for people with insomnia.
They also want to look at whether improving this waste-removal process could help people already experiencing dementia by reducing the buildup of harmful proteins in their brains.

articles.title: Japan's Teachers Struggling with Workloads
articles.intro: Explore the challenges Japanese teachers face with heavy workloads, overtime, emotional exhaustion, and the gap between policy and reality.

sentences.text: Teachers in Japan are overworked, struggling with excessive duties, and dealing with emotional exhaustion, according to a new survey.
The findings also show a major gap between working targets set by the government and the daily realities in Japanese schools.
Publishing company Shogakukan surveyed almost 2,700 education professionals between May and July this year.

By law, teachers should work no more than 8 hours a day, but according to the survey results, teachers are actually working an average of 11 hours per day, with 79% working at least 10 hours, and 24% working over 12 hours each day.
By law, teachers should also get at least 60 minutes of break time a day, but the results show that just 0.2% of teachers are getting this.
In fact, 65% said they took no breaks at all.
Many teachers also said having to take work home is normal.
Fifty percent said they take work home three or more days a week, while 86% said they have to work on their days off.
In 2025, the government set targets to reduce teachers' overtime hours.
However, teachers say this has resulted in pressure to hide their real overtime hours.
One teacher said it was frustrating to be told to leave work early, even though they hadn't finished their tasks.
Another said that teachers felt they either had to take work home so it wouldn't be counted as overtime, or change their time cards to hide the real hours they were working.
In fact, rather than cutting overtime hours, 61% said they would rather have their emotional exhaustion reduced.
Despite these problems, 68% said they wouldn't quit teaching because they found happiness in children's smiles, their growth and their achievements.

articles.title: UK Job Satisfaction Is at an All-Time Low
articles.intro: This lesson explores the decline in job satisfaction in the UK, reasons behind it, and its impact on employees and employers.

sentences.text: Most of us spend a large part of our lives at work, so it's important to feel happy with what we do!
But according to analysis from London's Resolution Foundation, many people in the UK are not satisfied with their jobs.
In fact, job satisfaction is at an all-time low.
The analysis is based on the 2025 British Social Attitudes survey, which had over {{prn:4,600|four thousand and six hundred}} participants.
The survey results were published on November 3 this year.
The data showed that just 74% of British workers are satisfied with their jobs.
This is the lowest percentage since the question was first asked in 1989.
When asked if they have an interesting job, just 63% said yes — a decrease of 11 percentage points from 10 years ago.
There are several reasons why people may be feeling less satisfied with their jobs.
Many workers feel their salaries aren't good, especially with rising costs in the UK and other parts of the world.
Others are unhappy with their working hours — 61% say they want more flexibility, up from 46% 10 years ago.
People are also less willing to do extra work for their employers.
Ten years ago, 69% of workers said they were happy to work harder to help their company.
Now it's just 55%.
According to the Resolution Foundation, this decrease in job satisfaction is bad news for both employees and employers.
And John Curtice, who worked on the British Social Attitudes survey, said employers may need to offer better pay and more flexible working hours to keep employees happy and motivated.

articles.title: How Dogs Could Help Japan Save $1 Billion a Year
articles.intro: This lesson explores how increasing dog ownership among older adults in Japan could reduce dementia risk and save nearly $1 billion in care costs.

sentences.text: Dogs are often called "man's best friend."
They give us company, love and a reason to get outside for a walk.
But could they also help save Japan almost $1 billion a year?
A new study suggests that increasing dog ownership among older people could help Japan reduce its long-term care costs.
Researchers believe dogs may help lower the risk of their owners getting dementia.
The study followed over 11,000 people in Tokyo aged 65 to 84 for seven-and-a-half years.
During that time, among people who never owned dogs, 18% developed dementia-related care needs.
Among dog owners, that fell to 13%.
Caring for people with dementia is expensive.
So if owning a dog helps lower the risk of dementia, it could save the Japanese government a lot of money.
Nine percent of people in the study owned dogs.

The researchers estimate that if dog ownership among older people across Japan increased to 13%, the country could save {{prn:150 billion|one hundred and fifty billion}} yen — almost {{prn:$1 billion|one billion dollars}} — each year in long-term care costs.
The study couldn't prove that owning a dog prevents dementia.
But there are reasons why having a dog might help.
Walking a dog can help owners stay active and give them more ways to meet other people.
Dogs also give their owners company and a daily routine.
And previous research suggests these things can help lower the risk of dementia.
But owning a dog as an older person isn't always easy.
What if an owner becomes ill or goes into the hospital?
Who will care for the dog?
The study's researchers say Japan needs more support for older dog owners, so they can enjoy life with their pets knowing someone will help care for them if needed.

articles.title: AI Boom Pushes China's Trade Surplus Past $1 Trillion
articles.intro: Explore how global demand for AI technology has boosted China’s trade surplus and the challenges this brings to its economy and trading partners.

sentences.text: China's trade surplus for the first 10 months of 2026 has risen above $1 trillion as investment in AI around the world drives its technology export market.
A trade surplus describes the situation where the value of a country's exports is higher than the value of what it imports from other countries.
In recent months, China — the world's second-largest economy after the US — has seen strong global demand for products used in AI technology, such as computer chips and data center servers.
And China's exports were worth 35% more in October 2026 compared with the same month last year.
In September 2026, they were worth 36% more than in September 2025.
If this strong export performance continues, with two more months left in the year, China could be on track for its highest-ever trade surplus.
It's already close to the record-breaking $1.2 trillion surplus it achieved across all 12 months of 2025.
There are obvious benefits to trade surpluses — they're good for employment and economic growth, and also strengthen a country's currency.
However, this trade surplus doesn't tell China's whole economic story.
China has operated with a trade surplus since the mid-1990s.
However, its domestic market is comparatively weak.
Chinese consumers save more and spend less money than those in many similarly large economies, saving an average of one-third of what they earn.
Weak domestic demand due to a consumer reluctance to spend means that China relies heavily on the export market, and this leaves it vulnerable to any slowdown in global demand.
Its export boom has also caused issues with trading partners like the US and the EU, which are now trying to limit Chinese products to protect their local businesses.
For example, talks between China and the EU last month saw the two parties agree to a limit on exports of Chinese-made hybrid vehicles to Europe.

articles.title: Shichi-Go-San: Japan's Special Day for Children
articles.intro: Learn about Japan’s Shichi-Go-San festival, its traditions, history, and how families celebrate the healthy growth of young children each November.

sentences.text: Every November, children across Japan dress up in their best clothes and visit shrines and temples with their families.
They do this to celebrate Shichi-Go-San, a traditional Japanese event for young children.
Shichi-Go-San means "seven-five-three" in Japanese.
The holiday celebrates girls aged three and seven, and boys aged three and five.
Families give thanks for their children's growth and pray for their future health.
The traditional date is November 15, but many families now celebrate on any weekend during November.
For Shichi-Go-San, children receive a special candy called _chitose ame_.
This long, thin candy is usually red or white, and its name means "thousand-year candy," representing the hope that children will live long, healthy lives.
The candy comes in colorful paper bags, often with pictures of cranes and turtles, because in Japan, these animals are symbols of long life and good luck.
Parents can buy this candy at supermarkets, and some shrines even give it to children as a gift when they visit.
Shichi-Go-San wasn't always a single event, however.
It's based on several different celebrations that wealthy Japanese families held in centuries past when their children reached certain ages.
At three, children could traditionally begin growing their hair instead of having it cut very short.
At five, boys wore traditional trousers, called _hakama_, for the first time.
And at seven, girls began wearing traditional kimono belts, called _obi_.
These ages were important because medical care was much more basic in the past, and many children died young.
So families wanted to celebrate their children reaching these ages.
Over time, these traditions came together and spread to ordinary families across Japan, and by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Shichi-Go-San had become a popular celebration.
Today, Shichi-Go-San is still an important family event.
Families continue to celebrate their children's growth and wish them a long, healthy life.

articles.title: Cyclists in Japan Receive 16,000 'Blue Tickets' in 6 Months
articles.intro: This lesson covers Japan's new blue ticket system for cycling violations, common offenses, fines, city data, and its impact on accident rates.

sentences.text: Police in Japan have recorded nearly 16,000 bicycle traffic violations since April, according to data from the country's National Police Agency (NPA).
On April 1 of this year, the NPA started using a new "blue ticket" system, which lets police quickly fine cyclists for breaking traffic rules.
In the system's first six months, using a smartphone while riding was the most common violation, making up 43% of all tickets.
Those caught riding while using a phone receive a fine of {{prn:12,000|twelve thousand}} yen, or about {{prn:$76|seventy six dollars}}.
The second most common violation was failing to stop when required, followed by riding through a red light.
Other common violations included entering a railroad crossing when the gate was down, and riding on the wrong side of the road.
These violations all carry fines of between {{prn:3,000|three thousand}} yen and {{prn:7,000|seven thousand}} yen — or between about {{prn:$19|nineteen dollars}} and {{prn:$44|forty four dollars}}.
The rules must be followed by all cyclists aged 16 and over.
Tokyo had the highest number of tickets, with nearly {{prn:3,000,|three thousand}} followed by Osaka with close to {{prn:2,900|two thousand and nine hundred}}.
Saitama recorded almost {{prn:1,900|one thousand and nine hundred}} violations, while Aichi had over {{prn:1,700|one thousand and seven hundred}}.
The NPA also said that bicycle accidents decreased by about 9% between April and September compared with the same time last year.
However, it said it's not clear if this is because of the new ticket system.

articles.title: Beijing's Palace Museum Named World's Most Visited
articles.intro: Explore how Beijing's Palace Museum became the world's most visited, trends in museum attendance, and the popularity of free museum entry worldwide.

sentences.text: Chinese museums were among the most visited in the world in 2025, with the Palace Museum in Beijing topping the list with 19 million visitors.

This is according to the Themed Entertainment Association's newest _Global Experience Index_, which found that the world's top 20 museums were visited 161 million times in 2025 — an increase of 5.4% from 2024.
The Palace Museum is in the center of Beijing, and housed in the city's old imperial palaces, also known as the Forbidden City.
The museum was opened 101 years ago, and inside it visitors can enjoy traditional Chinese art and relics.
In fact, Chinese museums took 12 places in the top 20.
And while the Palace Museum does charge about $6 to $9 for an adult ticket depending on the season, entry to more than 90% of museums in China is now free, making it easier for people to visit them.
For example, number six on the list is the Nanshan Museum in Shenzhen, and it's free to visit.
It offers a look at the city's history and local culture, and had 7.5 million visitors in 2025.
The National Museum of China, which is in Beijing, is also free to visit, and took 10th place on the list, with 6.9 million visits.
The most-visited museum outside of China was the Louvre in Paris.
It saw around 9 million visits last year — 3.5% growth compared with 2024 — putting it at number four on the list.
The Louvre isn't free, though, with tickets costing visitors from outside the European Union around $36.
London's Natural History Museum is free to visit, however, as are many of the British capital's museums.
It was number seven on the list — the only museum dedicated to the natural world in the top 20.

articles.title: Housing and Pay Protests Sweep Major Spanish Cities
articles.intro: Explore the causes and impact of housing and pay protests in major Spanish cities, focusing on rent increases and workers’ demands.

sentences.text: Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and public transport on Wednesday, November 11 before thousands took to the streets of major cities in a nationwide protest.
The walkout — under the slogan "Salaries. Housing. Prices." — was the first general strike in Spain in 14 years, and the first ever in which the main reason was housing.
Housing activists said 400,000 marchers joined the protest in Barcelona.
The city government also said that 55,000 people turned out just to walk behind one huge banner that read "Live. Not Just Survive."
Spanish government officials also estimated 120,000 people turned out in Madrid despite pouring rain.
Across Spain, average rents have more than doubled over the past decade, eating into household budgets and upsetting voters.

In Madrid, the average monthly cost of rent for a small apartment is around {{prn:$1,300|one thousand and three hundred dollars}}, while the national average monthly salary is around {{prn:$2,700|two thousand and seven hundred dollars}}.
That means the cost of renting an apartment in the Spanish capital is far more than the 30% of income recommended by housing experts.
Anger over rent increases recently reached boiling point after an 87-year-old woman named Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from an apartment where she'd lived for over 70 years.
Legal negotiations won Maricarmen the right to move back to her home, but she passed away shortly after.
Housing activists used the anger over Maricarmen's story to call for the strike, and soon won labor union support.
The housing activists want a number of measures introduced to protect renters, including the automatic renewal of leases.
Meanwhile, unions demand more public housing and a new minimum wage agreement.
The protests were mostly peaceful.
However, in Barcelona, some younger protesters were seen smashing the windows of brand-name stores and starting small fires on the Paseo de Gracia, a major shopping street.
Some launched fireworks at police.
There were also some scuffles between protesters and police in Madrid.
Police used pepper spray in some places and arrested 49 people for incidents related to the protests.

sentences.text: How strong do you like your matcha?
Well, in Japan, you'll soon be able to choose from five different strengths — all with the press of a button.
New vending machines are coming to Japan that make fresh matcha.
The machines are a little different from normal drink vending machines.
Instead of selling drinks in bottles or cans, they prepare each cup of matcha after the customer presses a button.
The idea is to give customers a drink that tastes like matcha made by hand.
The machines were made by two Japanese companies working together, Toyo Vending and Ito En.
Toyo Vending already makes vending machines that grind coffee beans and prepare each cup fresh.
Now, it's looking to bring similar technology to matcha.
Drinks company Ito En will supply the matcha powder, which is made from carefully chosen tea leaves.
Customers will be able to choose from five different strengths of matcha, as well as different drinks, including matcha lattes.
Matcha has become increasingly popular around the world.
In 2025, Japan exported 43% more green tea than the year before, partly because of growing demand for matcha.
And with more international tourists visiting Japan, Toyo and Ito En believe their machines will make it easier for visitors to try freshly prepared matcha.
The companies plan to put the machines in busy places, including train stations, airports, shopping areas, highway rest stops and areas that are popular with tourists.
The first machines are expected to appear this month, although no specific locations have been shared yet.
So for people who enjoy freshly made matcha, there'll soon be a new way to get a cup without going to a cafe!

articles.title: Tokyo Named World's Fourth Safest City to Visit
articles.intro: Explore how Tokyo was ranked among the world’s safest cities, the methodology behind the rankings, and which cities were deemed the safest for 2027.

sentences.text: Tokyo is one of the world's safest cities to visit, according to a new ranking.
Tokyo climbed up from ninth place last year to come fourth on this year's list, which ranks the world's safest cities for travelers in 2027.
Created by American travel insurance company Berkshire Hathaway Travel Protection, the ranking looked at 38 of the most popular cities with US travelers.

The company surveyed 1,500 travelers, and asked them to rank the cities for different aspects of safety, such as safety from crime and terrorism, health safety, transportation safety, and safety for women and minorities.
The survey results were then combined with safety rankings from _The Economist_ and online database Numbeo, as well as scores from travel safety site GeoSure.
Among participants in the Berkshire Hathaway survey, this year Tokyo was ranked second in the world for transportation safety — and with its famously well-run trains, that's little surprise!
The city was also third globally for safety from violent crime, and GeoSure gave it a very high score for safety at night.
However, it got lower survey scores for safety from terrorism and safety for women and minorities.
The world's safest city to visit in 2027 is Montreal, Canada.
Survey participants put Montreal first in the world for safety for women and minorities.
It was second for safety from violent crime and terrorism, second for health safety, and third for transportation safety.
After Montreal was Zurich, Switzerland.
Few survey participants had actually been there, but those who had visited gave it top scores for safety from violent crime and terrorism, and also for transportation and health safety.
Amsterdam in the Netherlands came third.
Berkshire Hathaway suggested that Amsterdam's relaxed attractions — such as walking around canals and seeing art — help to make it an especially safe place to visit.

For some people, doing laundry is a normal part of adult life.

The survey was done by Samsung with 2,000 adults in the UK.
It found that 80% of people have felt anxiety while doing laundry.
About half said they're afraid to wash certain clothes because they don't want to ruin them.

Others worry about how to wash vintage clothing — with 10% saying this has stopped them from buying vintage clothes altogether!

So why are people so anxious?
A little over half of participants said they've ruined something in the wash.

Almost two-thirds said that ruining something in the wash made them more anxious about washing other clothes.
But while many have laundry anxiety, others are the opposite.

Jenkins is an artist from the UK who is known for her knitted, crocheted and embroidered creations.
When she was a child, her grandmother taught her how to knit, and she has been creating things out of yarn ever since.
In the 1990s, she worked as a knitwear designer for big fashion houses, including Ralph Lauren and Marc Jacobs, and she later started her own fashion company.
When Jenkins needed a way to promote her company, she started knitting food, both for fun and to try to get people's attention.
That became her first food-themed exhibition, called "Comfort Food," in 2007.
Her food creations were so popular that they became a very important part of her career.
Since then, she's created collections based on bakeries, cafes, ice cream shops and more.
Her newest exhibition is called "Kate's {{prn:Knitalian|knitalian}}," which is made to look like an Italian restaurant.
It opened on October 30 at the Air Contemporary Gallery in London.
The exhibition has over 100 pieces made by Jenkins, including knitted plates of ravioli, bottles of wine and even a creamy tiramisu.
Jenkins wrote on her website that everything was made to look "deliciously real."
All pieces are available to buy, and the exhibition will be open until December 5.
Jenkins also likes to add a little humor to her work.

The "restaurant" has a sign saying that it's been rated by the "Stitchelin Guide" — instead of the Michelin Guide — and another that says it's on "Knitadvisor," instead of {{prn:Tripadvisor|trip advisor}}!

Few pizza toppings have caused as much disagreement as pineapple.

One Italian chef working in Australia is clearly in the second group.
Davide Tamburella was fired from La Costa restaurant in Brisbane in May this year after several disagreements with his bosses.
One was his refusal to make ham-and-pineapple pizzas for a large event.
Tamburella said adding the fruit to pizza was an "insult to his culture."
According to Australia's Fair Work Commission, it was the third time in four years that he had refused to make such pizzas.
The event was expected to bring in more than $10,000.
Restaurant owner Elliot Ingram said that although pineapple wasn't his favorite topping either, giving customers what they wanted was part of the job.
The restaurant had other complaints about Tamburella, however, including his language and behavior at work.
Tamburella later took his case to the commission, saying that he had been unfairly fired.
However, the commission rejected it because he had filed it too late.
La Costa closed in July, but Tamburella has since found work at another Brisbane restaurant.
And, perhaps unsurprisingly, pineapple pizza isn't on its menu.

articles.title: Many Americans 'Work Remotely' from the Office
articles.intro: Explore why many Americans go to the office only to work remotely, including research findings and reasons for this growing workplace trend.

sentences.text: Every morning, you wake up early, get ready in a hurry and make the long commute to the office — only to spend the next eight hours talking to colleagues through a screen.
According to a new report called _Remote Work from the Office_, this routine has become normal for many Americans.
Researchers from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the University of Virginia surveyed over {{prn:1,800|one thousand and eight hundred}} US workers in September this year.
On their most recent day in the office, nearly half had no in-person meetings.
Seventy-one percent were missing at least one teammate, while 15% had no casual face-to-face conversations with anyone.
And here's the interesting part: 37% joined at least one online meeting even though everyone taking part was in the same office.
"These workers commute in just to work remotely from the office," the researchers said.
So why is this happening?
One reason is that team members often work in different offices or cities, so even when employees show up, their colleagues may be far away.
Another is poor planning.
Some companies require a certain number of office days but let workers choose when to come in.
As a result, teammates often miss each other.
And some employees simply prefer video calls even when everyone is in the same office, because sharing screens can make it easier to work together.
Companies often say office time helps people share ideas, learn from one another and build relationships.
But just getting people through the office door may not be enough.

articles.title: First Cafe Opens at Tokyo's Imperial Palace
articles.intro: Learn about the first cafe to open inside Tokyo’s Imperial Palace, its unique offerings, and its connection to local history and culture.

sentences.text: Tokyo's Imperial Palace is one of the city's most famous places.
People like to go there to see the gardens and learn about Japan's history.
And now they can have a coffee there, too!
On November 3, a cafe opened at the Imperial Palace.
It's the first time a cafe has opened inside the palace grounds.
The cafe is part of Sarutahiko Coffee, a well-known coffee company in Tokyo.
It's inside the Ote Rest House, a new building in the palace's East Gardens.
Visitors can have their coffee inside the cafe or on the terrace on the second floor, which has nice views of the gardens.
The company made a new type of coffee just for this cafe, and visitors can also buy cakes and other sweet things.
Inside the new building, visitors can learn about the history of the Imperial Palace and the Imperial Family.
There's also a shop where visitors can buy souvenirs, or get some more coffee to make at home!
The cafe is near the Museum of the Imperial Collections.
This museum has been closed for seven years, but it opened again on November 3.
More than 2 million people visited the East Gardens in 2025.
You don't need to pay to go there — but you will have to pay for your coffee!

articles.title: Fender Creates Special Pokemon Guitars
articles.intro: This lesson covers Fender’s special edition Pokemon guitars for the 30th anniversary, their features, and how they celebrate classic Pokemon games.

sentences.text: In 1996, Game Boy players in Japan began their Pokemon adventures with the games _Pokemon Red_ and _Pokemon Green_.
Now, 30 years later, Pokemon Red and Green are back — but as guitars!
Guitar company Fender has released two special electric guitars in Japan for Pokemon's 30th anniversary.
And you can probably guess what colors they are!
The two guitars are based on different Fender guitars: the red guitar is a Stratocaster, and the green version is a Telecaster.
Both are among the company's best-known electric guitars, played by people like Buddy Holly, Jimi Hendrix and Keith Richards.
In the Pokemon games, red is often associated with Fire-type Pokemon, while green is associated with Grass types — so each guitar is also covered in lots of pictures of Pokemon from these two groups.
The fretboard of each guitar even has little Poke Balls as fret markers!
And if you push the top of the volume knob, the guitar adds a fuzz effect that makes it sound like 8-bit music, like the type used in those first Pokemon games.
Each guitar also comes with 11 red or green picks, each with different Pokemon characters.

The guitars each cost {{prn:396,000|three hundred and ninety six thousand}} yen — or about {{prn:$2,500|two thousand and five hundred dollars}} — and there's no information yet about how many will be sold.
For now, they're only being sold through a lottery to people in Japan.
People can enter the lottery through the Pokemon Center Online store in Japan between November 19 and November 24.
